notes:
I've written notes for most verses. There are some gaps. I only got to read a few sources: David Guzik's Enduring Word page (cut off after v. 21), and the commentary pages on Bible Hub and StudyLight for vv. 19, 21, 25 and 28. I found nothing from Catholic, Orthodox, NET Bible notes or Bible Odyssey sources. I also found nothing from prosperity or word-of-faith teachers. So vv. 10–18 and 22–33 have no notes or only thin ones.

**vv. 1–3: false reports, the crowd, the poor**
- v. 1: Guzik says you can only keep this command by actively stopping a false report. Staying neutral lets it keep spreading. He quotes Clarke: the person who invents a slander and the person who receives it are almost equally guilty. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-23/
- v. 1: Cole, quoted by Guzik, says "malicious witness" is better understood as a witness in a case about violence, because the verdict could cost the accused his life. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-23/
- v. 2: Guzik says it is easy and dangerous to go along with your peers and popular opinion. It becomes sin when doing so spreads a false report or twists justice. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-23/
- v. 3: Guzik says the poor are not to be favoured just for being poor, any more than the rich. The facts and the principles of justice should decide a case, not a person's social standing or perceived victim status. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-23/

**vv. 4–9: kindness and fair courts**
- vv. 4–5: Guzik sees this as a command to do good to your enemy. How you feel about someone does not decide what is right to do for them. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-23/ He quotes Cole that "enemy" here probably means the person you are in a legal dispute with. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-23/ He also links these verses to the parable of the Good Samaritan. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-23/
- v. 6: Guzik says being poor did not make someone right in a dispute, but it should never stop them getting a fair hearing. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-23/
- v. 7: Guzik reads "do not kill the innocent" as speaking to protecting life in the womb. He also takes it to mean that justice sometimes requires the death of the guilty. This is his own application. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-23/
- v. 8: Guzik notes that the command targets the person who takes the bribe, since bribes only work if someone accepts them. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-23/

**vv. 10–13: Sabbath year and Sabbath day**
- v. 11: Guzik says one purpose of the seventh-year rest was to feed the poor, who could gather what grew by itself on the resting land. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-23/
- v. 12: Guzik says Sabbath rest was meant for everyone, even animals. He compares this to the rest Jesus brings, which he says is for all people and all creation. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-23/

**v. 18: blood, leaven and fat**
- Guzik explains that leaven stood for sin and corruption, so the blood of a sacrifice could never be offered with leavened bread. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-23/
- On the fat, he says the whole sacrifice had to be given to God, with nothing kept back for later, especially the fat, which was the best part of the animal. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-23/

**v. 19: firstfruits, and the young goat in its mother's milk**
- Firstfruits: Ellicott says this means the very first crops to ripen. People tended to put off the offering, but real gratitude gives back as soon as it can. https://biblehub.com/exodus/23-19.htm
- The goat: there are three main readings.
  - **A pagan ritual.** Guzik and Cole call it a Canaanite fertility custom. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-23/ Constable says tablets found at Ras Shamra (ancient Ugarit) show this was a common Canaanite ritual. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/exodus/23-19.html
  - **A protest against cruelty.** The Pulpit Commentary finds no explanation satisfying except that the law protests against cruelty and against violating the bond between mother and young. https://biblehub.com/exodus/23-19.htm
  - **A food law.** Jewish tradition took it as a general ban on cooking meat with milk. GotQuestions argues this goes well beyond what the text says. https://www.gotquestions.org/not-boil-young-goat-mother-milk.html
- Some commentators push back on the ritual reading. They point out that Deut. 14:21 puts the same law in a list of food rules, so the goat was being cooked to eat. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/exodus/23-19.htm
- **Where Protestant teachers differ:**
  - Calvin (Reformed) thought eating meat cooked in milk could make people cruel, so God would not accept in sacrifice what was not allowed even at ordinary meals. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/exodus/23-19.html
  - Calvin also rejected the view that this was about not eating kids before they were weaned. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/exodus/23-19.html
  - Luther and others held exactly that view: it meant cooking a kid before it was weaned. This is reported by Keil & Delitzsch. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/exodus/23-19.htm
  - The Geneva Bible notes (Reformed) say it means no fruit should be taken before its proper time, which restrains cruel and greedy appetites. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/exodus/23-19.htm

**vv. 20–21: the angel who carries God's name**
- **The traditional reading: Christ before his birth.**
  - Guzik says this is Jesus appearing before the incarnation. He calls him the Second Person of the Trinity. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-23/
  - Matthew Henry finds this taught by Paul in 1 Cor. 10:9. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/exodus/23-21.htm
  - The Pulpit Commentary says God never puts his Name in a mere man, so this angel must be equal with God. https://biblehub.com/exodus/23-21.htm
  - Clarke also says the angel is most likely Christ, though some thought it meant Moses or Joshua. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/exodus/23-20.html
  - Justin Martyr, an early church writer, identified this angel with the Word (the Logos). https://biblehub.com/q/Why_is_the_angel_in_Exodus_23_20_important.htm
- **Another reading: God's authority, without saying it is Christ.**
  - The Geneva notes read "My name is in him" simply as God giving the angel his authority to rule in his name. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/exodus/23-21.htm
  - Keil & Delitzsch say God revealed himself in this angel, and they do not name Christ. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/exodus/23-20.html
  - Several modern Bible translations put the phrase as "my authority." https://biblehub.com/exodus/23-21.htm
- "He will not forgive rebellion": Gill argues this only makes sense if the angel *could* forgive sin, which only God can do. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/exodus/23-21.htm

**v. 22: blessing for obedience**
- Guzik says that under the law of Moses, blessing depended almost entirely on obedience. He says Christians are blessed in Jesus, not because they have obeyed, though sin still has consequences and God still corrects. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-23/

**vv. 25–26: blessing on food, and no sickness**
- An older commentary on Bible Hub says that if Israel had walked in God's ways, God would have protected them from all sickness by a miracle. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/exodus/23-25.htm
- The Geneva notes read "bread and water" as everything needed for this life. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/exodus/23-25.htm
- The Bible Hub study notes call the healing promise one of the blessings of Israel's covenant. They apply it today as encouragement to pray for health and trust God to heal. https://biblehub.com/study/exodus/23-25.htm
- Modern scholarship: the Cambridge Bible suggests vv. 23–25a may be a later addition to the text. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/exodus/23-25.htm

**v. 28: the hornet**
- Readings vary:
  - Calvin and Gill take it as real insects. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/exodus/23-28.html
  - Barnes takes it as a picture of terror. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/exodus/23-28.htm
  - Ellicott and the Pulpit Commentary suggest it was probably the Egyptians, who weakened the nations of Canaan. https://biblehub.com/exodus/23-28.htm
  - Augustine, cited by Keil & Delitzsch, saw it as the sharp stings of fear. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/exodus/23-28.htm
- F.B. Meyer says the same Presence that is an Angel to God's children becomes a hornet to the rebellious. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/fbm/exodus-23.html

**vv. 29–30: little by little**
- Matthew Henry applies this to the Christian life: God removes sin from his people's hearts gradually, not all at once. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/exodus/23-28.htm

**v. 33: the snare**
- Henry says that to keep away from bad ways, you must keep away from bad company. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/exodus/23-28.htm
